source_note: Whitney-Epstein, Hubbard, Dodson, Deflorio & Sissman, 'Optimizing Lead Distance', Wharton Sports Analytics Journal 2025, 25-slide presentation. Baseball base-stealing decision optimization: optimal lead from 1B when intending to steal 2nd, maximizing xRuns for base state 1-- via the printed linear-weight formula xRuns = 0.2*SB - 0.45*CS - 0.45*PK (Baseball Savant 2024 weights). A GLM on lead distance, pitcher Threat (Net Bases Prevented/100 IP), catcher pop time, and runner sprint speed outputs SB/CS/PK probabilities feeding xRuns; per-pitch only lead is controllable so the search holds other inputs constant and yields a per-situation optimum. Worked examples (Wheeler/Marchan/Ohtani -> 13.6 ft; Skenes/Crow-Armstrong/Grandal). Takeaway: leads typically too short, one more shuffle ~ +0.02 runs. Confounds: fear of basepath out, situational-vs-linear weights, new 3-pickoff rule. Extracted faithfully as a presentation artifact (not a derivative summary). Several result/player/team-evaluation slides (4, 11, 13, 17-20) are image-only figures whose numeric detail is not text-extractable and is deferred to the rendered slides; the GLM link/coefficients are prose-described, not printed, so the probability pipeline is reconstructed conceptually. The xRuns linear-weight formula is printed cleanly and used verbatim as LaTeX. Domain cs (sports decision optimization) matches catalog; baseball, not football. The linear-weight run-value objective, probability-to-value pipeline, ceteris-paribus marginal optimization, per-situation optimum, and behavioral/rule-change confounds are sport-agnostic and directly isomorphic to GSE's decision-optimization layer. No sportsbook lines/spreads/totals/implied odds in source or lifted into GSE.

reasoning_traces.think: The retrocausal genealogy of this deck is the application of linear-weight expected-run valuation to a single controllable baseball decision, the runner's lead off first base. Jack Whitney-Epstein, Jackson Hubbard, Lila Dodson, William Deflorio, and Zach Sissman, presenting at Wharton in 2025, pose a sharply scoped question: if a runner on first intends to steal second, what is the optimal lead, where optimal means maximizing expected runs for the base state with a runner on first only, using 2024 weights. The deck sits in the lineage of Baseball Savant's linear-weight run valuation and the broader expected-points tradition, translating a run-value objective into a concrete marginal decision. The three outcomes that matter are the stolen base, the caught stealing, and the pickoff, and the value of an attempt is the linear-weight sum xRuns equals 0.2 times stolen bases minus 0.45 times caught stealings minus 0.45 times pickoffs, so a steal adds a fifth of a run while either out subtracts nearly half a run. The recursive theory of mind is the probability-to-value optimization pipeline. A generalized linear model takes four inputs, the lead distance, the pitcher's Threat, the catcher's pop time, and the runner's sprint speed, and outputs the probabilities of a stolen base, a caught stealing, and a pickoff, which then feed the xRuns formula. Pitcher Threat is itself a rate statistic, net bases prevented per 100 innings pitched, measuring how well a pitcher suppresses the running game. The crucial modeling move is that for a single pitch only the lead distance is controllable, so the optimization holds Threat, pop time, and runner speed constant and searches over lead distance for the xRuns-maximizing value, and each pitcher-catcher-runner situation has its own optimum rather than a single league-wide number. Cross-layer veto adjudication is the gap between the mathematical optimum and the realized decision, and the caveats on the objective itself. The worked examples make the situation-dependence concrete: Wheeler at 1.803 Threat, Marchan at 1.87 seconds pop time, and Ohtani at 28.1 feet per second sprint speed yield an optimal lead of 13.6 feet, while a second example pairs the high-threat Skenes at 4.03 with the elite runner Crow-Armstrong at 30 feet per second and the slow-pop Grandal at 2.09 seconds, showing opposing forces on the optimal lead. The headline result is that leads are typically too short and that just one more shuffle is worth about plus 0.02 runs. But the deck honestly flags confounds: players' fear of making an out on the basepath keeps leads shorter than optimal, the linear weights are averages rather than situation-specific values, and the new rule limiting pitchers to three pickoffs changes the pickoff risk term. The implementation invariants map directly onto GSE. The linear-weight expected-run objective is GSE's run-value weighting of discrete outcomes; the GLM probability pipeline feeding that objective is GSE's outcome-probability-to-value chain; the hold-everything-else-constant marginal search is GSE's ceteris-paribus decision optimization; and the per-situation optimum is GSE's refusal to apply a single universal threshold. The fear-of-out confound is GSE's risk-aversion gap between optimal and realized behavior, and the situational-versus-linear-weights and three-pickoff-rule caveats are GSE's context-dependence and regime-shift vetoes. The outputs are expected-run values and optimal lead distances from public Baseball Savant data; GSE lifts no sportsbook lines, spreads, totals, or implied odds. The extraction caveat is that this is a slide deck, not a paper: several result and player/team-evaluation slides are image-only figures whose numeric detail cannot be extracted as text, and the GLM's exact link and coefficients are described in prose rather than printed as an equation, so the probability pipeline is reconstructed conceptually and the printed xRuns formula is the one verbatim equation. The invariant for GSE is to carry the linear-weight objective, the probability-to-value pipeline, and the per-situation marginal optimization while recording the image-figure limitation, the behavioral fear confound, and the rule-change regime shift before any quantitative reuse, treating the too-short-lead finding as a quantified inefficiency rather than a settled universal constant. The structure of the linear weights themselves carries a sovereign lesson for GSE. The asymmetry between the plus 0.2 for a stolen base and the minus 0.45 for either out means an out on the basepath costs more than twice what a successful steal gains, which is why the objective punishes caught stealings and pickoffs so heavily and why a merely average success rate is not enough to justify a attempt. A direct algebraic consequence of the printed formula, derived here rather than printed on the slides, is that the break-even success probability solves 0.2 p minus 0.45 times one minus p equals zero, giving p equals 0.45 over 0.65, about 0.692, so a runner must expect to succeed roughly sixty-nine percent of the time before the attempt is run-neutral. The lead-distance tradeoff is the mechanical heart of the optimization: a longer lead shortens the distance to second and raises the stolen-base probability, but it also enlarges the area the pitcher can pick off into and raises the pickoff probability, so the optimum balances these opposing marginal effects. The player and team evaluation slides then aggregate these per-pitch optimal-versus-actual gaps into a measure of how much run value a runner or a team leaves on the basepaths, which is the same realized-versus-optimal decision audit GSE runs on its own outputs.
